newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat calls for halt to Israeli settlement.
newsitem.headline: Arafat calls for halt to Israeli settlement.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat appealed to Middle East peace sponsors on Saturday to stop Israel building a Jerusalem settlement that threatens regional peacemaking.
Ignoring Israeli objections, diplomats from the United States, the European Union, Russia, Japan and Arab countries attended a one-day conference on the peace process called by Arafat in Gaza City.
"I called this meeting for one purpose which is to save the peace process," Arafat said in Arabic.

Asked after the three-hour meeting whether the crisis in Israeli-Palestinian relations could be defused, Arafat spokesman Marwan Kanafani said: "We are not optimistic at all. We will not stand with our arms folded."
Israel dismissed the Gaza meeting as a stunt and vowed to go ahead with the settlement between Arab East Jerusalem and Bethlehem next week, prompting fears of violence.

"The situation is really serious. What we are facing today from settlements in holy Jerusalem and in the rest of the Palestinian territories is a plan to destroy the peace process," Arafat said, opening the conference.

"President Arafat explained to the attendants the serious situation that the negotiations have reached after the recent Israeli decisions as regards settlements and redeployment," Kanafani told reporters. "The attendants will individually convey to the Israeli government these issues as they were addressed by the Palestinian side."

Arafat has been under pressure from colleagues and ordinary Palestinians to block the settlement that tightens Israel's grip on Jerusalem and weakens the Palestinian position in talks on the "final status" of the city. Those talks are scheduled to resume on March 17 but Palestinian officials said they doubted they would take place.

Palestinians see the decision to build 6,500 homes for Jews on the hill called Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic and Har Homa in Hebrew as an attempt to smother their hopes for an independent state with East Jerusalem as its capital.
Arafat said the decision violated interim peace deals by preempting the final status talks, which are supposed to reach a settlement of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict by 1999.
"I call upon the Israeli government to retract its settlement decisions and give the peace process the opportunity it deserves," Arafat said.
But Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh reaffirmed Israel's determination to break ground on the pine-covered hill.
"The prime minister made clear that work on Har Homa will begin next week," Naveh told Israel television. "If we bow to threats we will be unable to build in our capital in Jerusalem."
Israel views all of Jerusalem as its "eternal" capital.
Arafat also blasted Israel's unilateral decision to withdraw from 9.1 percent of the West Bank instead of the 30 percent he had wanted.
"We have become without a partner in this peace process...I call on the government of Israel to be a true partner and not to take one-sided decisions," Arafat said.
Israel said it was its right to determine the scope of each of three West Bank redeployments it must complete by the middle of next year under the Oslo self-rule accords with Arafat.

Naveh accused Arafat of manufacturing a crisis to put world pressure on Israel: "Yasser Arafat and the Palestinian leadership have a system...to create an atmosphere of crisis that may bring imminent violence."

The international community has censured Israel over its moves in Jerusalem. The U.N. General Assembly, by a vote of 130 to two, with two abstentions, called on Israel on Thursday to abandon the planned settlement.

The killing of seven Israeli schoolgirls by a lone Jordanian soldier on Thursday diverted much of the criticism Israel has faced over the plan. Some Israeli ministers said Arab warnings of crisis and violence were a factor in Thursday's shooting.
Jordan's King Hussein, who expressed shame and shock at the attack, was due in Israel on Sunday to deliver condolences to the bereaved Israeli families.
